phrases.translation: Ḥâ-Mĩm
phrases.explanation: These disconnected letters open the surah. The commentator says their explanation has already been given in earlier chapters, so he does not repeat it here, treating them as a known opening of revelation. The surah opens by swearing by the clear Book sent down to the Prophet. The surah keeps returning to the claim that worship belongs to God alone.

phrases.translation: By the clear Book
phrases.explanation: God swears by the clear Book He sent down to Muhammad. The commentator says reflecting on its lessons guides a person to the right path and proves it comes from a Wise and Praiseworthy One rather than being a human fabrication. Its first movement answers those who mocked earlier messengers in the same way. Its parables turn ordinary experience into a lesson about dependence on God.

phrases.translation: Certainly, We have made it a Quran in Arabic
phrases.explanation: God says He sent the Quran down in the language of the Arabs because those first warned by it were Arabs, so its meanings and admonitions would be intelligible to the people who heard it. The commentator repeatedly refers back to explanations given in earlier surahs. The surah honours those who fear God and hope in His mercy at the same time.

phrases.translation: so perhaps you will understand
phrases.explanation: The purpose of an Arabic revelation is that its hearers understand. The commentator notes it was not sent in a foreign tongue, which would have left them unable to grasp what it said. The chapter treats the Quran's Arabic wording as a mercy to its first hearers. The text gives space to doubt and excuse so that both can be answered.

phrases.translation: And indeed, it is—in the Master Record with Us—highly esteemed, rich in wisdom
phrases.explanation: The Quran is described as exalted and full of wisdom in the Mother of the Book with God. Reports explain that as the origin from which it was transcribed, and that its verses were made firm and then expounded. The fate of earlier deniers is offered as a warning to the Meccans. The chapter treats a person's own deeds as evidence no one can dispute.

phrases.translation: Should We then turn the ˹Quranic˺ Reminder away from you ˹simply˺ because you have been a transgressing people
phrases.explanation: The question is a threat, asking whether God should turn the punishment away from a transgressing people who rejected the Quran. The commentator prefers this reading because the following verses recount the fate of earlier deniers, and he notes two sound recitations. The reports disagree over some readings while agreeing on the main sense. Its final scenes show justice and mercy meeting in the same decree.

phrases.translation: ˹Imagine˺ how many prophets We sent to those ˹destroyed˺ before
phrases.explanation: God reminds the Prophet that many messengers were sent to the generations before him, just as he was sent to his own people, the Quraysh, so the pattern of rejection did not begin with them. The Prophet is consoled for the mockery he faces from his own people. The reports differ over details while leaving the main teaching unchanged.

phrases.translation: But no prophet ever came to them without being mocked
phrases.explanation: No prophet came to an earlier community calling to guidance without being mocked. The commentator says the Prophet's people are following the way of their predecessors, so their mockery should not weigh heavily on him. The section joins the Quran's divine origin to the accountability of those who reject it. The text insists that no soul carries another's burden, so each person answers for himself.

phrases.translation: So We destroyed those who were far mightier than these ˹Meccans˺.
phrases.explanation: God destroyed earlier mockers who were far stronger in violence than the Meccans, and their strength could not protect them from His might when His punishment came upon them. The surah opens by swearing by the clear Book sent down to the Prophet. The text treats the whole created order as belonging to the One who will judge it.

phrases.translation: The examples of ˹their˺ predecessors have ˹already˺ been related
phrases.explanation: The commentator explains that the example of the former peoples means the punishment that overtook them, so those who mock the Prophet should expect the same end for themselves. Its first movement answers those who mocked earlier messengers in the same way. The chapter treats arrogance as the response that turns guidance away.

phrases.translation: If you ask them ˹O Prophet˺ who created the heavens and the earth,
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told to ask the polytheists who created the seven heavens and the layers of the earth, brought them into being and produced them out of nothing. The commentator explains the roads as a mercy that makes travel and trade possible. Its closing words return to the knowledge of the Creator and Judge of all.

phrases.translation: they will certainly say, “The Almighty, All-Knowing did.”
phrases.explanation: They will answer that the Almighty, the All-Knowing created them, mighty in His sovereignty and vengeance and aware of everything within creation, with nothing at all hidden from Him. Rain that revives barren land is used as a proof of the resurrection. The text treats the measure of provision as a mercy rather than a limitation.

phrases.translation: ˹He is the One˺ Who has laid out the earth for you,
phrases.explanation: God spread out the earth as a resting place and a bed that people tread with their feet and walk upon with their legs. Riders are told to remember God's favour once they are settled on their mounts. The chapter contrasts the ease that forgets God with the hardship that calls on Him.

phrases.translation: and set in it pathways for you so that you may find your way
phrases.explanation: He also levelled roads in it for travel between cities for trade and livelihood. The reports call this a mercy, since without those paths people could not leave their lands or dwellings. The chapter treats everyday provision as evidence of the Creator's power. The reports name variant readings as equally sound rather than choosing one.

phrases.translation: And ˹He is the One˺ Who sends down rain from the sky in perfect measure, with which We give life to a lifeless land.
phrases.explanation: God sends rain from the sky in a measured amount suited to people's needs, not a devastating flood like the one sent on Noah's people nor so scant that vegetation fails, and with it revives barren land. Its signs move from the sky to the sea to the return of every person to God. The chapter shows that a warning refused until punishment arrives is too late.

phrases.translation: And so will you be brought forth ˹from the grave˺
phrases.explanation: The commentator says that just as rain brings dead earth back to life with crops, so people will be brought out of their graves alive after death, in the same form they had before. The section repeatedly calls on its hearers to use the understanding they were given. Its promises are described as promises God will not break.

phrases.translation: And ˹He is the One˺ Who created all ˹things in˺ pairs,
phrases.explanation: God created all things in pairs, setting male beings opposite female ones and female beings opposite male ones. The chapter asks the polytheists who created the heavens and the earth. The surah keeps joining belief in one God with the way a person lives and acts.

phrases.translation: and made for you ships and animals to ride
phrases.explanation: He also made ships for travel over the seas and cattle and beasts for travel over land, such as camels, horses, mules and donkeys, so people can reach the regions they need. It lists the earth, its roads, measured rain, paired creation, ships and cattle as signs. Its descriptions of the sea and the rain make divine power visible in ordinary life.

phrases.translation: so that you may sit firmly on their backs,
phrases.explanation: People are to settle firmly on the backs of the ships and animals He provided, riding them in safety on their journeys. The commentator explains the roads as a mercy that makes travel and trade possible. The surah treats guidance as a gift from God and straying as a loss to the person.

phrases.translation: and remember your Lord’s blessings once you are settled on them, saying,
phrases.explanation: Once settled, they should remember their Lord's favour and say words of praise, since the commentator treats the whole verse as an instruction to give thanks at the moment of riding. Rain that revives barren land is used as a proof of the resurrection. The chapter presents mercy as wider than the sinner's despair but not as permission to delay.

phrases.translation: “Glory be to the One Who has subjected these for us, for we could have never done so ˹on our own˺
phrases.explanation: Their confession is that God subjected these creatures to them, for they could never have mastered them by their own hands or strength. The reports gloss the phrase as not being able for it. Riders are told to remember God's favour once they are settled on their mounts. Its contrasts between the two groups are meant to be weighed, not merely admired.

phrases.translation: And surely to our Lord we will ˹all˺ return.”
phrases.explanation: The rider's declaration ends by affirming that everyone will return to their Lord after death, turning back to Him. The commentator reads it as part of the same act of remembrance. The chapter treats everyday provision as evidence of the Creator's power. The surah treats hardship as a call that people too quickly forget once it lifts.

phrases.translation: Still the pagans have made some of His creation out to be a part of Him.
phrases.explanation: The polytheists assigned God a share of His own creation by claiming that the angels were His daughters, which the reports describe as ascribing children to Him. The pattern of wealthy elites rejecting warners is traced through earlier communities. The text honours obedience that does not wait for a guaranteed outcome.

phrases.translation: Indeed, humankind is clearly ungrateful
phrases.explanation: The commentator says such a person is plainly ungrateful, denying the favours of his Lord in a way that becomes obvious to whoever reflects carefully on his condition. The section ends by pointing to the fate of those who denied their messengers. Its signs in creation are offered as evidence of the Creator, not as rivals to Him.

phrases.translation: Has He taken ˹angels as His˺ daughters from what He created,
phrases.explanation: The verse rebukes those who claim God took daughters from what He created, namely the angels, and calls it a reproach for their statement. The surah challenges the claim that the angels are God's daughters. The Quran is presented as a message whose warnings are repeated for a reason.

phrases.translation: and favoured you ˹O pagans˺ with sons
phrases.explanation: It asks whether He has favoured the pagans with sons while assigning daughters to Himself, exposing the inconsistency of a claim they would not accept for themselves. It exposes the inconsistency of men who dislike daughters for themselves. Its language of testimony, records and recompense makes judgment concrete.

phrases.translation: Whenever one of them is given the good news of what they attribute to the Most Compassionate,
phrases.explanation: When one of them is given the good news of the very thing he attributes to God, namely a daughter, he is dismayed by the news. The chapter asks whether the polytheists witnessed the creation they describe. The surah presents the Prophet as one who submits to what he was commanded.

phrases.translation: his face grows gloomy, as he suppresses his rage
phrases.explanation: His face darkens and he suppresses his rage, so the commentator notes they dislike for themselves exactly what they ascribe to their Lord. Their appeal to God's will is answered as conjecture without any revealed proof. The text insists that turning away from a message is a choice with a cost.

phrases.translation: ˹Do they attribute to Him˺ those who are brought up in fineries and are not commanding in disputes
phrases.explanation: The verse describes the being they assign to God as one raised amid ornaments who cannot argue clearly in a dispute, a description the reports applied to women. The commentator notes two well-known recitations of the phrase, both sound. The verse about a Book before the Quran denies that they have such a scripture. The chapter treats the unity of the prophets as a reason not to divide.

phrases.translation: Still they have labelled the angels, who are servants of the Most Compassionate, as female.
phrases.explanation: They called the angels, who are servants of the Most Compassionate, female. The commentator says two readings, one meaning those with Him and one meaning His servants, are both well known and correct. Inherited custom is presented as the real source of their idolatry. Its warnings are joined to an open invitation to turn back before judgment.

phrases.translation: Did they witness their creation? Their statement will be recorded, and they will be questioned
phrases.explanation: The verse asks whether they witnessed the angels' creation, and says their claim will be written down and they will be questioned about the lie they spoke. The pattern of wealthy elites rejecting warners is traced through earlier communities. Its questions are designed to be answered by the listeners themselves.

phrases.translation: And they argue, “Had the Most Compassionate willed, we would have never worshipped them.”
phrases.explanation: They argue that had God willed it they would never have worshipped the idols, and they take the delay of punishment as proof of His good pleasure with their worship. The section ends by pointing to the fate of those who denied their messengers. Its closing words gather the arguments of the surah into a single warning.

phrases.translation: They have no knowledge ˹in support˺ of this ˹claim˺. They do nothing but lie
phrases.explanation: The commentator replies that they have no knowledge, report from God, or proof for this claim. They speak only out of conjecture and falsehood. The surah challenges the claim that the angels are God's daughters. The text treats every messenger's warning as part of one continuous message.

phrases.translation: Or have We given them a Book ˹for proof˺,
phrases.explanation: The question asks whether God gave them a Book before the Quran containing the certain truth of what they claim about their idols. It exposes the inconsistency of men who dislike daughters for themselves. The chapter values a warning delivered plainly over a claim to special status.

phrases.translation: before this ˹Quran˺, to which they are holding firm
phrases.explanation: No such earlier scripture was given to which they could hold fast, act upon, and cite as proof against the Prophet. The chapter asks whether the polytheists witnessed the creation they describe. The chapter shows that human beings cannot flee the dominion of their Lord. The surah treats guidance as a gift from God and straying as a loss to the person.

phrases.translation: In fact, they say, “We found our forefathers following a ˹particular˺ way, and we are following in their footsteps.”
phrases.explanation: Their real argument is not revelation but inherited custom. They found their fathers following a way and simply follow in their footsteps, which the commentator explains as their practice of idol worship. Their appeal to God's will is answered as conjecture without any revealed proof. Its descriptions of the next life are meant to shape choices in this one.

phrases.translation: Similarly, whenever We sent a warner to a society before you ˹O Prophet˺, its ˹spoiled˺ elite would say,
phrases.explanation: The same pattern recurred whenever a warner was sent to an earlier town, since its wealthy leaders and great ones made the same reply to the messengers. The verse about a Book before the Quran denies that they have such a scripture. The surah treats the world's provision as a test that most people fail to recognise.

phrases.translation: “We found our forefathers following a ˹particular˺ way, and we are walking in their footsteps.”
phrases.explanation: They said their fathers had followed a religion and they were walking in their footsteps, a claim the surah goes on to show was made without any proof. Inherited custom is presented as the real source of their idolatry. Its warnings are addressed to people who already had access to revelation.

phrases.translation: Each ˹warner˺ asked, “Even if what I brought you is better guidance than what you found your forefathers practicing?”
phrases.explanation: Each warner asked whether they would still refuse if he brought them guidance better than the religion they had found their fathers practising. The pattern of wealthy elites rejecting warners is traced through earlier communities. The chapter shows that power belongs to God even when His servants appear weak.

phrases.translation: They replied, “We totally reject whatever you have been sent with.”
phrases.explanation: They answered by rejecting outright everything he had been sent with, so the commentator notes they denied the message rather than weighing its guidance. The section ends by pointing to the fate of those who denied their messengers. Its warnings are never separated from the possibility of forgiveness.

phrases.translation: So We inflicted punishment upon them.
phrases.explanation: God then took vengeance on those who denied their messengers by sending down His punishment upon those communities. The surah challenges the claim that the angels are God's daughters. The chapter treats the outcome of every dispute as belonging to God's final decision. The Quran is presented as a message whose warnings are repeated for a reason.

phrases.translation: See then what was the fate of the deniers
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told to consider the final fate of the deniers: destruction in this life by engulfing and drowning, then entry into the Fire, as a warning to others. It exposes the inconsistency of men who dislike daughters for themselves. The chapter asks readers to weigh a brief worldly advantage against its end.

phrases.translation: ˹Remember, O Prophet˺ when Abraham declared to his father and his people,
phrases.explanation: The surah recalls Abraham's declaration to his father and his people, who worshipped the same kinds of gods the Meccans worshipped. God explains that He let earlier generations enjoy life before sending the truth. The text treats the messenger's role as delivering the Book, not controlling the response.

phrases.translation: “I am totally free of whatever ˹gods˺ you worship
phrases.explanation: He announced that he was free of whatever gods they worshipped besides God, a disavowal the commentator links to the denial of the messengers before him. When the Quran came, they called it magic and rejected it outright. The chapter treats the denial of the Hereafter as the root of careless living.

phrases.translation: except the One Who originated me, and He will surely guide me.”
phrases.explanation: Abraham excepted the One who created him, who would guide him to the true religion. A report notes he used this wording because his people already admitted that God was their Lord. The demand for a great man from two cities is answered by God's sole choice. Its scenes of arrival show both groups receiving what they prepared for.

phrases.translation: And he left this enduring declaration among his descendants,
phrases.explanation: God made Abraham's declaration a lasting word among his descendants, identified in the reports with the testimony that there is no god but God. The chapter says He apportions livelihood and rank while reserving mercy for Himself. The surah asks its readers to consider what they would offer if judgment came.

phrases.translation: so they may ˹always˺ turn back ˹to Allah˺
phrases.explanation: Its purpose was that later generations among his posterity might always have someone who turned back to it after straying. Silver roofs and gold ornaments are described as a fleeting worldly enjoyment. The chapter treats sincerity as the measure of whether worship is genuine. Its questions are designed to be answered by the listeners themselves.

phrases.translation: In fact, I had allowed enjoyment for these ˹Meccans˺ and their forefathers,
phrases.explanation: God says He let the Meccans and their forefathers enjoy life without punishing their unbelief immediately, granting them a long respite. The section insists that the Hereafter belongs to those mindful of God. The surah treats patience under rejection as the Prophet's task while God decides the outcome.

phrases.translation: until the truth came to them along with a messenger making things clear
phrases.explanation: That respite lasted until the truth, meaning the Quran, came to them with a messenger who made things clear by proofs establishing that he was truly sent by God. The chapter turns to Abraham's disavowal of what his father and people worshipped. The chapter shows that idols cannot help, since harm and benefit belong to God.

phrases.translation: ˹But˺ when the truth came to them,
phrases.explanation: Yet when the truth and the messenger from God reached these polytheists, their response was outright rejection. His declaration is described as a lasting word among his descendants. Its accounts of Paradise and Hell give moral weight to ordinary decisions. The chapter values a warning delivered plainly over a claim to special status.

phrases.translation: they said, “This is magic, and we totally reject it.”
phrases.explanation: They called the Quran magic by which the messenger bewitched them and declared themselves disbelievers in it, denying that it could be from God. God explains that He let earlier generations enjoy life before sending the truth. The surah treats the whole world as the field of one divine judgment.

phrases.translation: And they exclaimed, “If only this Quran was revealed to a great man from ˹one of˺ the two cities!”
phrases.explanation: They objected that the Quran should have been sent down to a great man from Mecca or al-Ta'if. The reports name several wealthy notables they had in mind, though these are transmitted identifications rather than a settled one. When the Quran came, they called it magic and rejected it outright. The surah presents consultation and forgiveness as marks of the faithful.

phrases.translation: Is it they who distribute your Lord’s mercy?
phrases.explanation: The question rebukes them, asking whether it is they who apportion God's mercy and assign prophethood, or whether God gives that honour to whom He wills. The demand for a great man from two cities is answered by God's sole choice. The surah treats knowledge of the truth as a responsibility, not a privilege.

phrases.translation: We ˹alone˺ have distributed their ˹very˺ livelihood among them in this worldly life and raised some of them in rank above others so that some may employ others in service.
phrases.explanation: He already apportions their worldly livelihood, making some rich and others poor, some masters and others servants, so that people employ one another in service. The chapter says He apportions livelihood and rank while reserving mercy for Himself. The chapter treats gratitude as the proper response to relief after hardship.

phrases.translation: ˹But˺ your Lord’s mercy is far better than whatever ˹wealth˺ they amass
phrases.explanation: His mercy, including the choice of a messenger, is far better than the wealth they amass, since it comes from His granting rather than from their own choosing. Silver roofs and gold ornaments are described as a fleeting worldly enjoyment. The surah calls its readers to use reason when they consider the signs around them.

phrases.translation: Were it not that people might ˹be tempted to˺ become one community ˹of disbelievers˺,
phrases.explanation: Were it not that such luxury might make all people one community of disbelievers, preferring this life to their religion, God would have given it to them. The section insists that the Hereafter belongs to those mindful of God. The surah honours those who listen carefully and choose the better word.

phrases.translation: We would have supplied the homes of ˹only˺ those who disbelieve in the Most Compassionate with silver roofs and ˹silver˺ stairways to ascend
phrases.explanation: He would have roofed the houses of those who disbelieve in the Most Compassionate with silver and given them silver stairways by which to ascend. The chapter turns to Abraham's disavowal of what his father and people worshipped. The text treats trust in idols as a failure to recognise their powerlessness.

phrases.translation: as well as ˹silver˺ gates and thrones to recline on
phrases.explanation: He would also have supplied silver doors and couches of silver to recline on. The reports specify that both the doors and the couches in view would be made of silver. His declaration is described as a lasting word among his descendants. The surah treats revelation as a light given to someone who did not have it before.

phrases.translation: and ornaments ˹of gold˺. Yet all this is no more than a ˹fleeting˺ enjoyment in this worldly life.
phrases.explanation: Gold ornaments are added to the list, yet the commentator stresses that all of it is only a fleeting enjoyment of this life, with a transmitted warning against ostentatious display. God explains that He let earlier generations enjoy life before sending the truth. The text leaves room for uncertainty where the reports differ, rather than hiding it.

phrases.translation: ˹But˺ the Hereafter with your Lord is ˹only˺ for those mindful ˹of Him˺
phrases.explanation: The Hereafter with God is reserved instead for those mindful of Him, so lasting reward is not measured by the luxury a person had in the world. When the Quran came, they called it magic and rejected it outright. Its scenes of judgment reverse the confidence people placed in wealth or allies.

phrases.translation: And whoever turns a blind eye to the Reminder of the Most Compassionate,
phrases.explanation: Whoever turns away from the remembrance of God, neither fearing His power nor dreading His punishment, is described as looking with a weak and dim gaze. The Prophet is told he cannot make the deaf hear or guide the blind in heart. The surah treats death and resurrection as signs of the same power that created all things.

phrases.translation: We place at the disposal of each a devilish one as their close associate
phrases.explanation: God then assigns such a person a devil who tempts him and becomes his constant companion in this life. The threat against the deniers stands whether he lives to see it or not. The text treats the keys of provision and mercy as held by One hand alone.

phrases.translation: who will certainly hinder them from the ˹Right˺ Way while they think they are ˹rightly˺ guided
phrases.explanation: Those devils turn them away from the path of truth, making error attractive and faith in God hateful, while the people suppose they are rightly guided. The commentator calls this a state of doubt without insight. He is commanded to hold firmly to what was revealed to him. The chapter treats the Hereafter as the answer to a life that otherwise looks unfinished.

phrases.translation: But when such a person comes to Us, one will say ˹to their associate˺,
phrases.explanation: When such a person comes before God on Judgment Day, he will speak to the devilish companion that was assigned to him in the world. The section treats the Quran as an honour that brings a question with it. The surah keeps returning to the claim that worship belongs to God alone.

phrases.translation: “I wish you were as distant from me as the east is from the west! What an evil associate ˹you were˺!”
phrases.explanation: He will wish the distance between east and west lay between them and call him an evil associate. The reports note two recitations of the verb, close to each other in meaning. The surah describes those who turn a blind eye to the remembrance of God. Its parables turn ordinary experience into a lesson about dependence on God.

phrases.translation: ˹It will be said to both,˺ “Since you all did wrong,
phrases.explanation: Both are told that because they did wrong together, their sharing in the punishment will be of no benefit to them on that Day. A devil is assigned as a companion to the one who refuses to see the proofs. The surah honours those who fear God and hope in His mercy at the same time.

phrases.translation: sharing in the punishment will be of no benefit to you this Day.”
phrases.explanation: The commentator explains that sharing the torment lightens nothing, since each one of them bears his own complete portion of it. The companion makes error attractive while the person thinks he is guided. The text gives space to doubt and excuse so that both can be answered.

phrases.translation: Can you make the deaf hear,
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is asked whether he can make the deaf hear, meaning those from whom God has withheld the hearing of the proofs set out in the Book. The chapter records the regret such a person will feel when he meets his Lord. The chapter treats a person's own deeds as evidence no one can dispute.

phrases.translation: or guide the blind or those clearly astray
phrases.explanation: Nor can he guide the blind in heart or those in clear error. The commentator says turning hearts belongs to God alone, not to the messenger who delivers the warning. The Prophet is told he cannot make the deaf hear or guide the blind in heart. Its final scenes show justice and mercy meeting in the same decree.

phrases.translation: Even if We take you away ˹from this world˺,
phrases.explanation: Even if God takes the Prophet away from this world before the threat is carried out, the threat itself does not lapse. The threat against the deniers stands whether he lives to see it or not. The reports differ over details while leaving the main teaching unchanged.

phrases.translation: We will surely inflict punishment upon them
phrases.explanation: He will still take vengeance on the deniers. The reports differ over whether this refers to the Quraysh or to later generations within the Prophet's own community. He is commanded to hold firmly to what was revealed to him. The text insists that no soul carries another's burden, so each person answers for himself.

phrases.translation: Or if We show you what We threaten them with, We certainly have full power over them
phrases.explanation: Or God may show the Prophet during his lifetime the victory He promised him over them, since He has full power to grant it. The commentator prefers this reading because the passage is addressed to the polytheists. The section treats the Quran as an honour that brings a question with it. The text treats the whole created order as belonging to the One who will judge it.

phrases.translation: So hold firmly to what has been revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺.
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is commanded to hold firmly to what his Lord revealed to him, namely the commands and guidance that this Quran enjoins upon him. The surah describes those who turn a blind eye to the remembrance of God. The chapter treats arrogance as the response that turns guidance away.

phrases.translation: You are truly on the Straight Path
phrases.explanation: He is assured that he is on a straight and rightly guided path, identified in the reports as Islam, the religion God enjoined on His servants. A devil is assigned as a companion to the one who refuses to see the proofs. Its closing words return to the knowledge of the Creator and Judge of all.

phrases.translation: Surely this ˹Quran˺ is a glory for you and your people.
phrases.explanation: The Quran is described as an honour for the Prophet and for his people, the Quraysh, to whom it was sent down among them. The companion makes error attractive while the person thinks he is guided. The text treats the measure of provision as a mercy rather than a limitation.

phrases.translation: And you will ˹all˺ be questioned ˹about it˺
phrases.explanation: They will all be questioned about what they did with it, whether they followed what their Lord commanded and abstained from what He forbade. The chapter records the regret such a person will feel when he meets his Lord. The chapter contrasts the ease that forgets God with the hardship that calls on Him.

phrases.translation: Ask ˹the followers of˺ the messengers that We already sent before you
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told to ask those sent before him, which the commentator explains as asking the scriptures of the earlier messengers and the believers among the People of the Book. The Prophet is told he cannot make the deaf hear or guide the blind in heart. The reports name variant readings as equally sound rather than choosing one.

phrases.translation: if We ˹ever˺ appointed ˹other˺ gods to be worshipped besides the Most Compassionate
phrases.explanation: The question is whether God ever appointed other gods to be worshipped beside Him. No messenger came to any people with such a command. The threat against the deniers stands whether he lives to see it or not. The chapter shows that a warning refused until punishment arrives is too late.

phrases.translation: Indeed, We sent Moses with Our signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs,
phrases.explanation: God sent Moses with His proofs to Pharaoh and the notables of his people, just as He sent the Prophet to the polytheists of the Quraysh. The chapter says his people followed him because their hearts were sealed. Its promises are described as promises God will not break.

phrases.translation: and he said: “I am a messenger of the Lord of all worlds.”
phrases.explanation: Moses announced that he was the messenger of the Lord of all worlds, matching the claim the Prophet had made to his own people. His drowning is made a lesson for every generation that comes after. The surah keeps joining belief in one God with the way a person lives and acts.

phrases.translation: But as soon as he came to them with Our signs, they laughed at them
phrases.explanation: When Moses brought the signs proving his call to God's oneness and the rejection of idols, Pharaoh and his people laughed at them. The commentator calls this a consolation to the Prophet, whose people mocked him in the same way. The surah recalls Moses being sent with signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs. Its descriptions of the sea and the rain make divine power visible in ordinary life.

phrases.translation: although every sign We showed them was greater than the one before.
phrases.explanation: Every sign God showed them was greater in proof and more compelling than the one that preceded it, further establishing the truth of Moses' message. Earlier messengers are said to have taught the same oneness of God. The surah treats guidance as a gift from God and straying as a loss to the person.

phrases.translation: Ultimately, We seized them with torments so that they might return ˹to the Right Path˺
phrases.explanation: Yet He seized them with torments, identified in the reports as years of drought, failing crops, locusts, lice, frogs and blood, so that they might turn back from disbelief to obedience. Each sign shown to Pharaoh's people was greater than the one before. The chapter presents mercy as wider than the sinner's despair but not as permission to delay.

phrases.translation: ˹Then˺ they pleaded, “O ˹mighty˺ magician!
phrases.explanation: In distress they pleaded with Moses, addressing him as a mighty magician, a form of speech the reports explain as acknowledging his mastery rather than accusing him of sorcery. The torments are described as a call to return before the final punishment. Its contrasts between the two groups are meant to be weighed, not merely admired.

phrases.translation: Pray to your Lord on our behalf, by virtue of the covenant He made with you. We will certainly accept guidance.”
phrases.explanation: They asked him to pray to his Lord by virtue of the covenant that the plague would be lifted if they believed, promising to accept guidance, a promise the next verse says they broke. Pharaoh pleaded through Moses when the plague was upon them, then broke his word. The surah treats hardship as a call that people too quickly forget once it lifts.

phrases.translation: But as soon as We removed the torments from them, they broke their promise
phrases.explanation: As soon as God removed the torment from them, they broke their promise and returned to their error. The reports describe this as acting treacherously and persisting in corruption. His boast rests on Egypt's rivers, his own eloquence and the lack of gold bracelets. The text honours obedience that does not wait for a guaranteed outcome.

phrases.translation: And Pharaoh called out to his people,
phrases.explanation: Pharaoh proclaimed to his people, the Copts, in a boast meant to strengthen his claim against Moses and to persuade them of his own superiority. The chapter says his people followed him because their hearts were sealed. Its signs in creation are offered as evidence of the Creator, not as rivals to Him.

phrases.translation: boasting, “O my people! Am I not sovereign over Egypt as well as ˹all˺ these streams flowing at my feet? Can you not see
phrases.explanation: He claimed sovereignty over Egypt and the rivers and gardens flowing before him, asking whether they could not see the affluence and good fortune he enjoyed. His drowning is made a lesson for every generation that comes after. The Quran is presented as a message whose warnings are repeated for a reason.

phrases.translation: Am I not better than this nobody who can hardly express himself
phrases.explanation: He contrasted himself with Moses, whom he called contemptible and barely able to make his speech clear. The reports mention a defect in Moses' tongue and note Pharaoh's pride in his own eloquence and stature. The surah recalls Moses being sent with signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs. Its language of testimony, records and recompense makes judgment concrete.

phrases.translation: Why then have no golden bracelets ˹of kingship˺ been granted to him
phrases.explanation: He asked why no golden bracelets of kingship had been cast upon Moses if he were truly a messenger from the Lord of the worlds. Earlier messengers are said to have taught the same oneness of God. The surah presents the Prophet as one who submits to what he was commanded.

phrases.translation: or angels come with him as escorts!”
phrases.explanation: He also demanded why no angels came with him as escorts, treating visible wealth and a royal retinue as the signs by which prophethood should be recognised. Each sign shown to Pharaoh's people was greater than the one before. The text insists that turning away from a message is a choice with a cost.

phrases.translation: And so he fooled his people, and they obeyed him.
phrases.explanation: Pharaoh made his people lightheaded with such words and they obeyed him, believing him and declaring Moses a liar rather than weighing his signs. The torments are described as a call to return before the final punishment. The chapter treats the unity of the prophets as a reason not to divide.

phrases.translation: They were truly a rebellious people
phrases.explanation: The commentator says they were a defiantly disobedient people, abandoned by God and sealed in their hearts, which is why they followed him. Pharaoh pleaded through Moses when the plague was upon them, then broke his word. Its warnings are joined to an open invitation to turn back before judgment.

phrases.translation: So when they enraged Us,
phrases.explanation: The commentator explains the phrase about their enraging God as their provoking His wrath and indignation by persistent denial. His boast rests on Egypt's rivers, his own eloquence and the lack of gold bracelets. Its questions are designed to be answered by the listeners themselves. The chapter shows that a warning refused until punishment arrives is too late.

phrases.translation: We inflicted punishment upon them, drowning them all
phrases.explanation: So God punished them and drowned them all, an end the reports connect to their mockery of the signs and their rejection of every warning. The chapter says his people followed him because their hearts were sealed. Its closing words gather the arguments of the surah into a single warning.

phrases.translation: And We made them an example and a lesson for those after them
phrases.explanation: God made them a bygone vanguard and an example for those who came after them. The reports gloss it as a lesson and admonition, and the commentator prefers the well-known reading that means predecessors. His drowning is made a lesson for every generation that comes after. The text treats every messenger's warning as part of one continuous message.

phrases.translation: When the son of Mary was cited as an example ˹in argument˺,
phrases.explanation: When the son of Mary was cited as an example, one report linking it to the creation of Adam without a father, the Meccans seized on the comparison. A comparison involving Mary's son becomes the occasion for a sharp dispute. The chapter values a warning delivered plainly over a claim to special status.

phrases.translation: your people ˹O Prophet˺ broke into ˹joyful˺ applause
phrases.explanation: They broke into clamour about it, some reports saying they accused the Prophet of wanting them to worship him as the Christians worshipped Jesus. The reports differ over which comparison the Meccans were making. The chapter shows that human beings cannot flee the dominion of their Lord.

phrases.translation: They exclaimed, “Which is better: our gods or Jesus?”
phrases.explanation: One report has them asking which is better, their gods or Jesus, saying they would be content for their idols to share the fate of Jesus, Ezra and the angels. Jesus is described as a favoured servant, not a son of God. Its descriptions of the next life are meant to shape choices in this one.

phrases.translation: They cite him only to argue. In fact, they are a people prone to dispute
phrases.explanation: The commentator says they raised the comparison only to dispute, not to seek truth, and transmits a saying that no people stray without being given contentiousness. The surah says God could replace human beings with angels on the earth. The surah treats the world's provision as a test that most people fail to recognise.

phrases.translation: He was only a servant We showed favour to,
phrases.explanation: Jesus was only a servant among God's servants whom He favoured with success and faith, not a son of God as the Christians claimed. The pronoun about the Hour is read by many as referring to Jesus and by others to the Quran. Its warnings are addressed to people who already had access to revelation.

phrases.translation: and made as an example for the Children of Israel
phrases.explanation: God made him a sign and a proof for the Children of Israel by sending him to them to call them to their Lord, so the verse clears him of their claim. Satan is named as the sworn enemy who turns people from obedience. The chapter shows that power belongs to God even when His servants appear weak.

phrases.translation: Had We willed, We could have easily replaced you ˹all˺ with angels,
phrases.explanation: God says that had He willed, He could have destroyed the children of Adam and replaced them with angels on the earth who would worship Him there. Jesus is reported to have commanded fear of God, obedience and worship of Him alone. Its warnings are never separated from the possibility of forgiveness.

phrases.translation: succeeding one another on earth
phrases.explanation: The reports note a second understanding of the phrase about succeeding one another on earth, meaning one generation following after another. The section warns the groups who differed about him of a painful Day. The chapter treats the outcome of every dispute as belonging to God's final decision.

phrases.translation: And his ˹second˺ coming is truly a sign for the Hour.
phrases.explanation: The commentator records a difference over the pronoun: many refer it to Jesus, whose appearance or descent is a portent by which the Hour is recognised, while others referred it to the Quran. A comparison involving Mary's son becomes the occasion for a sharp dispute. The chapter asks readers to weigh a brief worldly advantage against its end.

phrases.translation: So have no doubt about it, and follow me. This is the Straight Path
phrases.explanation: The reciters agreed on the reading meaning knowledge, and the verse commands people not to doubt the Hour but to follow God's path, explained as obeying His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. The reports differ over which comparison the Meccans were making. The text treats the messenger's role as delivering the Book, not controlling the response.

phrases.translation: And do not let Satan hinder you, ˹for˺ he is certainly your sworn enemy
phrases.explanation: Satan must not be allowed to turn people from obedience to God, for he is an open enemy whose hostility was shown in his refusal to prostrate to Adam and in the deception that drove Adam from Paradise. Jesus is described as a favoured servant, not a son of God. The chapter treats the denial of the Hereafter as the root of careless living.

phrases.translation: When Jesus came with clear proofs,
phrases.explanation: Jesus came to the Children of Israel with clear proofs, which a report identifies with the Gospel, and with wisdom understood in this place as prophethood. The surah says God could replace human beings with angels on the earth. Its scenes of arrival show both groups receiving what they prepared for.

phrases.translation: he declared, “I have come to you with wisdom, and to clarify to you some of what you differ about. So fear Allah, and obey me
phrases.explanation: He said he had come to clarify some of the matters they disputed about and commanded them to fear God and obey him in what he brought. The pronoun about the Hour is read by many as referring to Jesus and by others to the Quran. The surah asks its readers to consider what they would offer if judgment came.

phrases.translation: Surely Allah ˹alone˺ is my Lord and your Lord,
phrases.explanation: Jesus declared that God alone is his Lord and theirs, the One who has the right to be acknowledged as deity and obeyed sincerely. Satan is named as the sworn enemy who turns people from obedience. The chapter treats sincerity as the measure of whether worship is genuine.

phrases.translation: so worship Him ˹alone˺. This is the Straight Path.”
phrases.explanation: He commanded them to worship Him alone without assigning any partner, calling that the straight path and the only religion God accepts from His servants. Jesus is reported to have commanded fear of God, obedience and worship of Him alone. The surah treats patience under rejection as the Prophet's task while God decides the outcome.

phrases.translation: Yet their ˹various˺ groups have differed among themselves ˹about him˺,
phrases.explanation: The groups differed among themselves about Jesus. The reports name the disputing parties among the Children of Israel, or alternatively the Jews and the Christians. The section warns the groups who differed about him of a painful Day. The chapter shows that idols cannot help, since harm and benefit belong to God.

phrases.translation: so woe to the wrongdoers when they face the torment of a painful Day
phrases.explanation: Woe is pronounced on those who did wrong through that dispute, because the torment of a painful Day awaits them for it. A comparison involving Mary's son becomes the occasion for a sharp dispute. Its accounts of Paradise and Hell give moral weight to ordinary decisions.

phrases.translation: Are they waiting for the Hour to take them by surprise when they least expect ˹it˺
phrases.explanation: The question asks whether those disputing factions are waiting for anything other than the Hour, which will begin the Resurrection suddenly while they perceive nothing at all of its coming. The reports differ over which comparison the Meccans were making. The surah treats the whole world as the field of one divine judgment.

phrases.translation: Close friends will be enemies to one another on that Day, except the righteous
phrases.explanation: On that Day close friends will become enemies of one another, each disowning the other, except those whose friendship was built on the fear of God rather than shared disobedience. Jesus is described as a favoured servant, not a son of God. The surah presents consultation and forgiveness as marks of the faithful.

phrases.translation: ˹who will be told,˺ “O My servants! There is no fear for you Today, nor will you grieve—
phrases.explanation: To the God-fearing it will be said: O My servants, no fear for you today, nor grief. The commentator notes the call is addressed broadly so that others may hope until the believers are specified. Paradise is described with golden platters, cups, desired delights and abundant fruit. The surah treats knowledge of the truth as a responsibility, not a privilege.

phrases.translation: ˹those˺ who believed in Our signs and ˹fully˺ submitted ˹to Us˺
phrases.explanation: Those addressed are the ones who believed in God's signs, held His Book and His messengers to be true and acted on what the messengers brought, submitting as upright people on the religion of Abraham. The commentator says the Garden is inherited through the deeds people did. The chapter treats gratitude as the proper response to relief after hardship.

phrases.translation: Enter Paradise, you and your spouses, rejoicing.”
phrases.explanation: They are told to enter Paradise with their spouses, rejoicing in the honour God has given them. One report glosses the word for rejoicing as tasting delight in what their Lord bestowed. Hell is described as a torment that is never lightened and ends in despair. The surah calls its readers to use reason when they consider the signs around them.

phrases.translation: Golden trays and cups will be passed around to them.
phrases.explanation: Golden platters, described in the reports as bowls, and cups will be passed around among them as they sit in the Garden. The plea to Malik for an end is met with the answer that they must remain. The surah honours those who listen carefully and choose the better word.

phrases.translation: There will be whatever the souls desire and the eyes delight in. And you will be there forever
phrases.explanation: There they will have whatever their souls desire and whatever delights their eyes, and they will remain in that state forever. The section closes by insisting God did them no wrong, they wronged themselves. The text treats trust in idols as a failure to recognise their powerlessness.

phrases.translation: That is the Paradise which you will be awarded for what you used to do
phrases.explanation: This is the Paradise given to them as an inheritance for the good deeds they used to do in the world. A report says it is the portion of the people of the Fire, transferred to the believers. The Hour is said to arrive suddenly while people are unaware of it. The surah treats revelation as a light given to someone who did not have it before.

phrases.translation: There you will have abundant fruit to eat from
phrases.explanation: There will be abundant fruit of every kind in Paradise, of which they may eat whatever they desire whenever they wish. Friendships built on disobedience will turn into enmity on that Day. The text leaves room for uncertainty where the reports differ, rather than hiding it.

phrases.translation: Indeed, the wicked will be in the torment of Hell forever
phrases.explanation: The evildoers, who committed the crime of disbelief against God in the world, will abide perpetually in the punishment of Hell without ever leaving it. The God-fearing are welcomed with a call that removes fear and grief. Its scenes of judgment reverse the confidence people placed in wealth or allies.

phrases.translation: It will never be lightened for them,
phrases.explanation: The punishment will never be eased or lightened for them at any time, however long they remain there. Paradise is described with golden platters, cups, desired delights and abundant fruit. The surah treats death and resurrection as signs of the same power that created all things.

phrases.translation: and there they will be overwhelmed with despair
phrases.explanation: They will be overwhelmed with despair in it, the commentator explaining the word as one who has abandoned hope of deliverance and surrendered to the torment. The commentator says the Garden is inherited through the deeds people did. The text treats the keys of provision and mercy as held by One hand alone.

phrases.translation: We did not wrong them, but it was they who were the wrongdoers
phrases.explanation: God did them no wrong by punishing them. Rather they wronged themselves by worshipping what they were not obliged to worship and by denying His oneness and His signs. Hell is described as a torment that is never lightened and ends in despair. The chapter treats the Hereafter as the answer to a life that otherwise looks unfinished.

phrases.translation: They will cry, “O Mâlik! Let your Lord finish us off.”
phrases.explanation: They will cry to Malik, the keeper of Hell, asking him to let his Lord put an end to them so that they might die and be done with the torment. The plea to Malik for an end is met with the answer that they must remain. The surah keeps returning to the claim that worship belongs to God alone.

phrases.translation: He will answer, “You are definitely here to stay.”
phrases.explanation: He will answer that they are there to stay. The reports add that he makes them wait a long time before replying, material the exegete transmits without building doctrine on it. The section closes by insisting God did them no wrong, they wronged themselves. Its parables turn ordinary experience into a lesson about dependence on God.

phrases.translation: We certainly brought the truth to you,
phrases.explanation: God says He brought the truth to the Quraysh through the messenger He sent them, namely Muhammad and what he came with. The Hour is said to arrive suddenly while people are unaware of it. The surah honours those who fear God and hope in His mercy at the same time.

phrases.translation: but most of you were resentful of the truth
phrases.explanation: Yet most of them detested the truth he brought, resenting it rather than accepting it, which is why the warning stands against them. Friendships built on disobedience will turn into enmity on that Day. The text gives space to doubt and excuse so that both can be answered.

phrases.translation: Or have they mastered some ˹evil˺ plan?
phrases.explanation: The question asks whether the polytheists have firmly resolved on some settled scheme against the truth that was brought to them. The phrase about offspring is explained as an idiom of denial rather than a condition. The chapter treats a person's own deeds as evidence no one can dispute.

phrases.translation: Then We ˹too˺ are surely planning
phrases.explanation: God says He too is resolving firmly, settling for them what will disgrace and humiliate them through punishment. A report has Mujahid say that if they devise evil, He devises its like. God is glorified far above the lie that He has a child. Its final scenes show justice and mercy meeting in the same decree.

phrases.translation: Or do they think that We do not hear their ˹evil˺ thoughts and secret talks?
phrases.explanation: Or do they imagine that God does not hear the thoughts they hide from people and the secret counsel they take among themselves? The chapter declares that He alone is God in the heavens and on the earth. The reports differ over details while leaving the main teaching unchanged.

phrases.translation: Yes ˹We do˺! And Our messenger-angels are in their presence, recording ˹it all˺
phrases.explanation: He does hear it, and His messenger-angels are present with them, writing down every word they utter and every speech they make. Knowledge of the Hour is said to rest with Him alone, along with all dominion. The text insists that no soul carries another's burden, so each person answers for himself.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “If the Most Compassionate ˹really˺ had offspring, I would be the first worshipper.”
phrases.explanation: The commentator records several readings. The phrase is an Arabic idiom of denial meaning the Most Compassionate has no child and the speaker is the first to affirm and worship that truth, while another reading makes him the first to reject their claim. The Prophet's complaint about his people is recorded and confirmed by God. The text treats the whole created order as belonging to the One who will judge it.

phrases.translation: Glorified is the Lord of the heavens and the earth,
phrases.explanation: God is glorified as Lord of the heavens and the earth, an acquittal and exaltation above every blemish in the Possessor of all creation. The surah ends with a command to turn away in peace and leave the outcome to Him. The chapter treats arrogance as the response that turns guidance away.

phrases.translation: the Lord of the Throne, far above what they claim
phrases.explanation: He is Lord of the Throne that encompasses everything, far above the lie of their attributing a child to Him and above every other false description. The surah asks whether the polytheists have settled some scheme against the truth. Its closing words return to the knowledge of the Creator and Judge of all.

phrases.translation: So let them indulge ˹in falsehood˺ and amuse ˹themselves˺ until they face their Day, which they have been warned of
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told to leave those who invent lies against God to their idle talk and play in this life until they meet the Day they were promised, identified with the Day of Resurrection and their punishment. It insists God hears their secret talk and that angels record every word. The text treats the measure of provision as a mercy rather than a limitation.

phrases.translation: It is He Who is ˹the only˺ God in the heavens and ˹the only˺ God on the earth.
phrases.explanation: He is the only God worshipped in the heavens and the only God worshipped on the earth, with nothing else deserving worship beside Him. The phrase about offspring is explained as an idiom of denial rather than a condition. The chapter contrasts the ease that forgets God with the hardship that calls on Him.

phrases.translation: For He is the All-Wise, All-Knowing
phrases.explanation: He is the All-Wise and All-Knowing, so worship is to be devoted exclusively to Him and no partner is to be ascribed to Him. God is glorified far above the lie that He has a child. The reports name variant readings as equally sound rather than choosing one.

phrases.translation: And Blessed is the One to Whom belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth and everything in between!
phrases.explanation: Blessed is the One whose dominion covers the seven heavens, the earth and everything between them, where His judgment holds sway and His decree is carried out. The chapter declares that He alone is God in the heavens and on the earth. The chapter shows that a warning refused until punishment arrives is too late.

phrases.translation: With Him ˹alone˺ is the knowledge of the Hour.
phrases.explanation: With Him alone is the knowledge of the Hour when the Resurrection begins and creatures are gathered from their graves to the place of Reckoning. Knowledge of the Hour is said to rest with Him alone, along with all dominion. Its promises are described as promises God will not break.

phrases.translation: And to Him you will ˹all˺ be returned
phrases.explanation: To Him all people will be brought back after death, returning to Him so that He may requite them for what they did. The Prophet's complaint about his people is recorded and confirmed by God. The surah keeps joining belief in one God with the way a person lives and acts.

phrases.translation: ˹But˺ those ˹objects of worship˺ they invoke besides Him have no power to intercede,
phrases.explanation: Those whom the polytheists invoke beside God have no power of intercession with Him for anyone at all. The surah ends with a command to turn away in peace and leave the outcome to Him. Its descriptions of the sea and the rain make divine power visible in ordinary life.

phrases.translation: except those who testify to the truth knowingly
phrases.explanation: The exception is for those who testify to the truth knowingly, professing His oneness with certainty. The commentator says this includes angels, Jesus and Ezra by His permission, unlike the idols. The surah asks whether the polytheists have settled some scheme against the truth. The surah treats guidance as a gift from God and straying as a loss to the person.

phrases.translation: If you ask them ˹O Prophet˺ who created them,
phrases.explanation: If the Prophet asks the polytheists who created them, they will answer that God created them, admitting the very point they otherwise resist. It insists God hears their secret talk and that angels record every word. The chapter presents mercy as wider than the sinner's despair but not as permission to delay.

phrases.translation: they will certainly say, “Allah!” How can they then be deluded ˹from the truth˺
phrases.explanation: The verse asks how, having admitted that, they can be turned away from worshipping their Creator and deprived of attaining the truth about His worship. The phrase about offspring is explained as an idiom of denial rather than a condition. Its contrasts between the two groups are meant to be weighed, not merely admired.

phrases.translation: ˹Allah is Aware of˺ the Prophet’s cry: “O my Lord! Indeed, these are a people who persist in disbelief.”
phrases.explanation: The verse records the Prophet's cry complaining to his Lord that his people do not believe. The commentator says two well-known recitations are both correct in meaning and that God confirmed his saying as true. God is glorified far above the lie that He has a child. The surah treats hardship as a call that people too quickly forget once it lifts.

phrases.translation: So bear with them and respond with peace. They will soon come to know
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told to turn away from them and say a word of peace, a greeting with an implied upon you, because they will soon know. The reports note a variant reading that addresses them directly. The chapter declares that He alone is God in the heavens and on the earth. The text honours obedience that does not wait for a guaranteed outcome.
